newsitem.title: USA: Ecuador dealt blow in Texaco enviro case.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador dealt blow in Texaco enviro case.

text.p: A U.S. judge dealt another blow to the plaintiffs in a long-running environmental lawsuit against Texaco Inc.

U.S. District Court Judge Jed Rakoff Tuesday denied a request by the Ecuadoran government and state owned oil company Petroecuador to intervene in support of the plaintiffs, said Henry Dahl, an attorney representing the Ecuadoran government.
On November 12, Rakoff dismissed the class action suit against Texaco, saying the U.S. was not the appropriate forum for the case.
The Ecuadoran government and Petroecuador sought to express formal support for the plaintiffs in an effort to clear up a record of conflicting signals from Quito on the case.
The move was also intended to persuade the judge to reconsider his earlier ruling.
The judge is expected to reiterate this decision at a meeting scheduled for 1800 EST/2300 GMT Wednesday.
"The issue tonight (in the U.S. court) is whether or not the (Ecuadoran) government can intervene," said Patrick Kim, a law clerk in the judge's chambers.
The plaintiffs are not giving up. They filed a motion for reconsideration in the case in the same U.S. District Court in New York and filed the intervention papers as an appendix.

"The Republic of Ecuador has been denied the right to intervene in the case directly. However, its views will be known, indirectly, through the attachment included in plaintiff's motion for reconsideration," Dahl said in a statement.
They also plan to appeal in the Second Circuit U.S. Appeals Court in New York if Judge Rakoff upholds his ruling.

Meanwhile, the U.S. government has expressed concern about the Ecuadoran government's recent efforts to invalidate Texaco's nearly completed environmental remediation plan in the areas where it operated.
Deputy Chief of Mission Curt Struble at the U.S. Embassy in Ecuador met Tuesday with Ecuadoran Attorney General Leonidas Plaza Tuesday to discuss the government's efforts to anul the plan.
"Unilateral attempts to abridge contracts doesn't exactly build confidence among investors," said Mark Krischik, the U.S. embassy's public affairs officer.

Texaco operated in Ecuador from 1964 to 1992, and has said the case should be resolved in Ecuadoran courts. Texaco is charged with environmental degradation tied to its exploration and production activities in Ecuador's Amazon region.
